definition: A set of prompts, formats, and practice structures that let learners engage repeatedly and voluntarily with cases while receiving guidance, feedback, or decision support.
description: This cluster represents a resource that makes practice easy to enter, repeat, and use on the learner’s own terms: optional access to cases, self-directed repetition or skipping, timed challenges with feedback, and visible prompts such as SBAR or AM I HERO NOW. In realist terms, the resource appears to work by inviting engagement and reducing uncertainty during decision or referral tasks, which is reflected in outcomes such as greater readiness to report abnormalities, reduced fear during referral, more time spent on test items, and repeated practice to mastery. The same resource also appears in shadowing, serious games, and video-based or test-enhanced cases where learners can follow, decide, or revisit material repeatedly.

definition: A set of instructional and feedback resources that expose, correct, and help learners work through diagnostic errors in case-based reasoning.
description: This cluster represents resources used to make diagnostic mistakes visible and actionable: error cases, worked examples, feedback, and seminars that focus attention on incorrect feature identification, unresolved reasoning errors, and the correct solution. In realist terms, these resources are offered in contexts where learners have limited knowledge, underdeveloped illness scripts, or cases that exceed their current capacity, and they are intended to trigger self-monitoring, bias checking, and stronger concept links rather than simple answer recall. Their significance is that they aim to reduce diagnostic error by supporting learners to notice, compare, and revise reasoning across similar cases and complex tasks.

description: This cluster represents instructional resources that scaffold learners’ reasoning through case-based prompts, examples, feedback, and opportunities to review reasoning pathways. definition: Structured prompts, examples, feedback, and case materials that are designed to steer learners toward building, querying, and refining schemas during clinical reasoning tasks.
description: This cluster represents a family of instructional supports that intervene in how learners approach diagnosis: they prompt an initial hypothesis, provide worked or peer examples, offer item-level feedback, and supply structured case summaries or key-feature e-seminars. In realist terms, these resources are intended to trigger more cognitive resources into schema construction and back-tracing of abnormalities, which can reduce incorrect feature identification and improve structured knowledge, although the studies also show that such support does not always outperform nonanalytic or explicit combined instruction. The significance of the cluster is that it links teaching format to the learner’s reasoning process and diagnostic performance across domains such as arterial hypertension, dermatology, and biliary disease.

definition: A cluster of study outcomes showing that prompts, examples, supervision, and feedback can improve diagnostic reasoning and performance, especially when cases are unfamiliar.
description: This community captures the observed effects of reasoning-support interventions on learners’ diagnostic work: self-explanation prompts, resident or near-peer examples, justification and mental-model prompts, supervised consultation, and immediate feedback are associated with better diagnostic accuracy, improved performance, and sometimes longer analytic response times. The pattern is not uniform across contexts: benefits are stronger in unfamiliar cases and may be absent in familiar cases or specific case types, with some studies showing reduced engagement and elaboration when cases are already familiar. In realist terms, the shared outcome is improved reasoning performance following supports that invite explanation, comparison, and consideration of alternatives.

definition: A set of training or task features that present cases through paired images, labels, videos, or simplified prompts that steer learners toward rapid similarity-based diagnosis rather than explicit analytic listing.
description: This cluster represents resources that cue learners to make diagnoses by comparing surface features, using labelled exposure, or following simplified decision paths instead of constructing an analytic table. In the CMO logic, these resources appear to trigger more efficient nonanalytic responses, sometimes improving performance on unfamiliar cases, but they can also be associated with lower diagnostic accuracy relative to analytic reasoning when the task demands more explicit analysis. The shared significance is that the studies repeatedly use structured prompts and case formats to shape how learners attend to and process diagnostic information.

definition: Prompting or case-design features that steer learners toward a particular diagnostic route or response, often by introducing a prior answer, a suggested diagnosis, or a strategy cue.
description: This cluster represents intervention features that shape how novice ECG diagnosticians approach a case: biasing feature presentation, incorrect diagnostic suggestions, whatever-strategy-comes-naturally prompts, and intended greater non-analytic reliance. The shared function across the studies is not the diagnosis itself but the way the prompt or case framing channels the learner’s response.

definition: A set of teaching and task-design features that deliberately structure diagnostic reasoning practice through paired examples, case-based tasks, simulated or timed cases, and feature-focused support.
description: This cluster represents interventions that organize diagnostic learning by combining explicit instruction with structured practice formats such as annotated normal/abnormal image pairs, contrastive learning, structured case-based reasoning, simulated ward environments, and timer-based case solving. In realist terms, these are resources offered to learners to shape how they approach diagnosis, but the cluster also includes signals that the combined instruction can be confusing and may produce poorer immediate diagnostic performance when the task demands or assessment framing are not well aligned. Its significance is that it captures a family of intervention designs aimed at directing reasoning processes rather than simply testing them, with some members explicitly challenging the use of decision speed as a valid assessment parameter.
